A few years ago I purchased my dream knife. A Spyderco Endura Sprint Run Damascus [more pictures in comments]
I know little to nothing about knives...What differentiates this one from others and makes it your dream knife, apart from aesthetics?

Well, I've always wanted a genuine Damascus steel knife. You can purchase knives that look like they're made from Damascus steel, but, 90% of the time they're just a single piece of stainless steel that has had a pattern laser etched on the surface. This knife is made of 36 layers of folded stainless steel with a VG-10 core. Giving it the Damascus look with the VG-10 edge giving you the best of both worlds in one.

They make other Damascus knives but they've got brown, titanium, or carbon fiber handles. I prefer this jiggered camel bone blue. I feel it better complements the look of the blade.

We've all heard about how Richard Price printed Instagram photos on canvas and sold them for 90,000$.

Art is a strange thing. I don’t pretend to understand it, even though I have called myself an artist at various points in my life.

For those who value and buy art, there is more than just the physical product. The artist’s intent and purpose gives it value.

Value is a social contract, a man-made concept. If I hand you a piece of paper and say it is worth $90,000, and you agree with me, then the paper is worth $90,000 to the both of us. It doesn’t make all other similar pieces of paper worth $90,000, just this one. Other people may not agree, but then those losers don’t have a piece of paper worth $90,000, do they?

I think, even if rhetorically, you pointed out the wrong person as being the looser. Art is what we define it to be, sure if an ad from craigslist is a socially acceptable form of art then so be it. But I refuse to recognize it.

Yes, I was joking about everyone else being losers. But I don’t think the two people in my example are losers either; they just value a thing differently.

Value is not just in money. There is also aesthetic value, whether the work is pleasing to the eye; cognitive value, whether the work makes you think, engages with you mentally and not just visually; moral value, whether the work promotes moral norms, or is perverse or amoral; and probably some other things that they teach in art philosophy class.

I don’t think those photos were worth $90,000, but it has caused you to think, and led to this discussion. So even though we reject the monetary value, Richard Price’s work did add value to our lives.
